oneSentence: The delay between sending a request to a model and receiving its reply, or the next part of that reply.
plainExplanation:
Latency is the waiting time. In a chat system, it usually means how long it takes from your prompt being sent until the first word appears, or until the full reply arrives.

What goes in is a request: your prompt, the earlier conversation, and system instructions. The service then prepares that text, runs the model, and starts generating output one token at a time. A token is a small piece of text, such as a word, part of a word, or punctuation.

What happens inside can take longer for several reasons. A longer prompt gives the system more text to process. A larger model may take more computation per token. Network delay, server load, safety checks, and tools such as web search can also add waiting time.

What comes out is the model's response, often streamed gradually. Latency is about delay, not quality. A fast answer can still be wrong, and a slower answer is not automatically better.

Latency is often confused with throughput. Latency asks, "How long do I wait for one reply?" Throughput asks, "How many replies or tokens can the system produce in a period of time?"

everydayAnalogy.title: Planning a journey across a city
everydayAnalogy.story: You ask a journey desk in Nairobi how to get from the airport to a meeting venue during heavy traffic. The staff member first reads your note, checks the map, looks at the time of day, and compares two routes. A few seconds later, they begin speaking with the first step, then continue with the rest of the directions. Your waiting time before hearing the answer, and the pace of the directions after that, are the parts that match latency.

mapping.analogyElement: The staff member reading the note and checking the map

mapping.analogyElement: The pause before the first direction is spoken
The pace of the rest of the directions
mapping.aiElement: Rate at which output tokens are generated

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A human journey clerk may reason with real-world knowledge, ask clarifying questions on their own, or choose to stay silent. A language model does not work like a person giving directions. It generates text token by token based on patterns from training and current input. Also, real travel time and response latency are different things: latency is only the waiting time for the answer, not the quality or usefulness of the route.

visual.title: Where waiting time comes from in a model reply
visual.learningObjective: Show that response time is the sum of several delays before and during generation, and that long prompts or extra tools can increase it.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. Each box names one stage that adds delay: send request, prepare input, generate first token, generate remaining tokens. Small notes under boxes show common causes such as network delay, long context, model size and tool use. Read from left to right as a timeline.

steps.label: 1. Send request
steps.explanation: The user's prompt and conversation history travel to the service. Network distance and congestion can add a small delay before processing starts.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a message bubble entering the first box. Add a thin clock icon below with the note 'network'.

steps.label: 2. Prepare input
steps.explanation: The system formats instructions, checks safety rules, and breaks text into tokens. Longer context usually means more work before generation begins.
steps.visualInstruction: Second box shows stacked text lines turning into small token blocks. Add note 'prompt length, safety checks'.

steps.label: 3. Generate first token
steps.explanation: The model computes the first piece of output. This often shapes the delay users notice most, because it is the moment the reply first appears.
steps.visualInstruction: Third box shows a model chip icon and one token appearing. Add emphasis ring and note 'time to first token'.

steps.label: 4. Generate the rest
steps.explanation: The model continues producing tokens one by one until the reply ends. The speed here affects how quickly the full answer arrives.
steps.visualInstruction: Fourth box shows a row of tokens extending rightward. Add note 'tokens per second, tools may pause output'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each box to reveal one short note about what can increase delay: long context, large model, server load, tool calls, or slow network.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains response time as a timeline with four stages. First, the request travels to the service, where network delay can add waiting time. Second, the service prepares the input by formatting instructions, applying checks and turning text into tokens; longer conversation history increases this work. Third, the model generates the first token, which determines when the reply first becomes visible. Fourth, it generates the remaining tokens one by one, which affects how long the full answer takes. The main lesson is that waiting time comes from several stages, not one single cause.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-step horizontal timeline shows the same stages without animation: send request, prepare input, generate first token, generate remaining tokens. Short notes under each step list common causes of delay.

workedExample.scenario: The officer asks an approved assistant to draft three bullets from cleared, aggregate staffing updates for the donor report. The service log records when the request arrives, when the first words appear and when the final bullet is complete.
workedExample.input: A prompt plus the cleared staffing narrative and aggregate figures.
process: The request travels to the service and may wait in a queue.
The service processes and tokenises the prompt, applies required checks and retrieves any authorised supporting material.
The model generates the first visible words. The elapsed time to this point is the time to first token.
The model continues generating until the final bullet is complete. The total elapsed time is the time to last token.
workedExample.result: Both measurements are latency. One describes the wait before the reply starts; the other describes the wait for the complete reply. They can change independently, for example when retrieval delays the start or a longer answer extends generation.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At a shared services centre, a human resources officer is finalising the staffing narrative for a quarterly progress report to a donor. The front office wants it by close of business. An approved internal assistant is asked to turn cleared, aggregate recruitment updates into three concise points. The officer sees how long the tool takes to begin replying and how long it takes to finish.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The first delay determines whether the tool feels responsive. The time until the complete answer arrives determines whether it actually saves time before clearance. A longer prompt, retrieval from approved files, policy checks, server load and the length of the requested answer can affect either measure.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Human resources material may contain personal, medical or performance information. Do not enter such material into any tool that has not been approved for it. Even in an approved system, use only authorised content, remove unnecessary identifiers and follow the applicable access and retention controls.

whyItMatters:
Latency affects whether a tool feels usable in practice. If replies arrive quickly, people can keep their place in a task such as drafting, searching or comparing options. If replies are slow, users may rush, repeat prompts, or stop trusting the workflow.

For non-specialists, latency helps with practical choices. A short prompt may return faster than a long one. Turning on extra tools, adding many documents or using a larger model may increase waiting time. That can be acceptable for a careful background task, but less suitable in a live meeting or urgent support setting.

It also helps to ask the right question. If a team says a system is "slow", the issue might be network delay, time to first token, full-answer time, or server load. Those are related, but not identical.

In a procurement unit’s technical evaluation of bids
At a service review after an internal assistant slows near close of business
In a performance discussion between a country office and Headquarters

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Lower latency means the model is more accurate.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. Latency measures waiting time, not truthfulness or suitability. A system can answer quickly and still produce an incorrect or misleading completion. Accuracy depends on many other factors, including the prompt, context, model and whether tools are used well.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Latency is only caused by a slow internet connection.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Network delay is only one part. Time is also spent preparing the input, applying checks, running the model, generating tokens and sometimes calling external tools. A fast connection cannot remove those steps.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: One latency number tells the whole story.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Often there are at least two useful numbers: time until the first token appears and time until the full answer finishes. A service may feel responsive on the first measure but still take a long time to complete a long reply.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is how long you wait after asking the model something before you start seeing the answer, or before the whole answer is finished.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In large language model systems, latency usually refers to elapsed time between request submission and one or more output milestones, commonly time to first token and time to last token. It can include network transit, request queuing, prompt processing, tokenisation, safety or policy checks, retrieval or tool calls, and autoregressive generation during inference. Prompt length, context window use, model size, hardware, batching and server load can all change it. This differs from throughput, which measures how many requests or tokens a system can handle per unit time.

keyTakeaway: Latency may mean the wait until the first words appear or the wait until the reply is complete. Neither measure tells you whether the answer is good.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes latency in a chat assistant?
options: How long you wait from sending a prompt until the reply starts or finishes
How many facts in the reply are correct
How many users can log in at the same time
How much training data the model originally used
quickCheck.explanation: Latency is about delay. In chat systems, people often care about both time to first token and time to full response. Correctness, user capacity and training data are different questions.

issues.problem: The analogy says the pace of the directions matches latency, then maps that pace to the rate at which output tokens are generated. A generation rate is throughput under the page's own distinction. The rate can affect full-response latency, but it is not itself latency.
issues.fix: End the story with: "Your waiting time before hearing the answer, and the total time until the directions end, are the parts that match latency." Replace the final mapping with: analogyElement "The time until all directions have been spoken" and aiElement "Time until the full response is received".

issues.problem: The limitation does not correct the analogy's central confusion between output pace and latency. It should state that speaking pace corresponds to throughput and only affects the latency of the completed response.
issues.fix: A human journey clerk may reason with real-world knowledge, ask clarifying questions on their own, or choose to stay silent. A language model instead generates text token by token from patterns in training and the current input. The speaking pace corresponds to output throughput, not latency by itself. It affects the latency until the full reply arrives. Real travel time is separate from response latency.

issues.problem: The visual equates the model generating its first token with the reply becoming visible. A service may buffer tokens, and delivery or display can add delay after generation. The diagram therefore omits part of visible time to first token while claiming to show where response time comes from.
issues.fix: Replace the step explanation with: "The model computes the first piece of output. Buffering, delivery and display can add more delay before it appears to the user." In the accessibility description, replace the third-stage sentence with: "Third, the model generates the first token; buffering and delivery can delay when it becomes visible."

issues.problem: The quiz does not test the stated distinction from throughput. The three distractors are unrelated enough that the answer is obvious without understanding latency. Each current option was considered: option 0 correctly describes latency; option 1 describes correctness; option 2 describes login capacity; option 3 describes training data. Only option 0 is defensible, but the distractors are weak.
issues.fix: Replace option 2 with: "How many tokens the system produces per second". Keep correctOptionIndex as 0 and revise the explanation to distinguish this throughput measure explicitly.
